issues.legal_issue: A workshop falls within the statutory definition of a coal mine when it is in or adjacent to the mine and is used substantially for the mine, with whether it is in substance part of the mine determined from the circumstances.
material_facts: The owner operated a workshop on a plot adjacent to a coal mine, and whether the workshop was substantially used for the mine was disputed.
The workshop was also said to have conducted business for third parties, and its accounts and relationship to the mine were contested.
issues.conclusion: The location and substantial-use requirements for a workshop are conjunctive. A different plot number, a compound wall, or third-party work does not alone exclude a workshop from the mine; whether it is in substance part of the mine depends on the circumstances. The Court did not decide whether this workshop met the test.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(h)(vii) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 requires a workshop to be in or adjacent to a mine and used substantially for the mine or mines under the same management. The Court treated the inquiry into substantial use as an inquiry into whether the workshop pertains to, or in substance is part of, the mine; the value of work for the mine compared with work for others is not determinative. The enlarged definition in section 2(h) covers assets connected with the integrated mining activity.

rule.if: coal_mine_asset_classification and asset_is_workshop and located_in_or_adjacent_to_mine and substantially_used_for_mine

predicates.coal_mine_asset_classification: The dispute concerns whether an asset forms part of a coal mine for purposes of a nationalisation proceeding.
predicates.asset_is_workshop: The asset being classified is a workshop.
predicates.located_in_or_adjacent_to_mine: The workshop is located in or adjacent to the coal mine.
predicates.substantially_used_for_mine: The workshop is substantially used for the purposes of the mine or mines under the same management.

issues.definition: When a coal-mine asset classification concerns a workshop that is in or adjacent to the mine and substantially used for it, the workshop forms part of the nationalised mine.

issues.legal_issue: A seriously disputed factual question about whether property vested as part of a nationalised mine cannot be resolved in a constitutional writ proceeding and must be adjudicated through an appropriate civil proceeding.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether the engineering unit was in or adjacent to the mine and substantially used for it.
The parties also disputed whether the bungalow and guest house were solely used for mine officers and staff, and whether the properties otherwise fell within the statutory definition of a mine.
The High Court declined to decide whether the properties were covered by that definition because the dispute raised a serious question of title.
issues.conclusion: The disputed property-title questions could not be decided in proceedings under Article 226; the proper remedy was a suit. The parties later consented to an arbitrator adjudicating their disputes, and the Court directed that course.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(h) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 specifies the kinds of property included in a mine, but the Act provides no special machinery for deciding whether a particular asset answers that description. Where the facts are seriously controverted and the dispute is one of title, the matter is a civil dispute for adjudication in a civil court, rather than determination under Article 226.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A party seeks resolution of the property dispute through a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.seriously_disputed_property_facts: The parties seriously contest the facts bearing on the property's relationship to the mine or its use.
predicates.asset_vesting_depends_on_fact_finding: Whether the property vested as part of the mine depends on resolving those disputed facts.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ proceeding concerns seriously disputed property facts that determine whether an asset vested, the title dispute requires civil adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: During the statutory accounting period, the government has the exclusive right to collect money due to a coal mine and may use it to meet mine liabilities, while money not collected by the end of that period may be realised directly by the former owner.
material_facts: The management of the mines was taken over before nationalisation, and the former owners alleged that substantial amounts from debtors and coal sales remained outstanding.
The parties disputed whether the government could collect money after the appointed day and whether former owners could directly recover amounts that remained unrealised by the specified date.
The statutory scheme provided a specified date for government collections and payments, and made pre-appointed-day liabilities the former owners’ responsibility.
issues.conclusion: Under sections 19(3) and 19(4), read with section 18(2), the government could exclusively receive mine money realised up to the specified date and apply it to the relevant liabilities. Amounts not realised by the government by that date could be realised directly by former owners to meet their pre-existing liabilities.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18(2) and 19(3)–(4) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 form an integrated accounting scheme. Section 19(3) authorises collection up to the specified date notwithstanding that the realisation relates to an earlier period, and section 19(4) authorises discharge of liabilities that could not be discharged by the appointed day. Section 7 leaves pre-appointed-day liabilities with the former owners. The Court also considered the relationship between the Nationalisation Act and the Coal Mines (Taking over of Management) Act, 1973, under which management was taken over while title initially remained with the owners.

predicates.nationalisation_management_accounting_pr: The dispute concerns accounting for a coal mine after government management and nationalisation.
predicates.mine_money_remains_to_be_collected: Money due to the mine remains to be collected after the appointed day.
predicates.pre_transfer_mine_liabilities_exist: Liabilities relating to the mine existed that could not be discharged by the appointed day.

issues.definition: In a mine-management accounting dispute, if mine money remains to be collected and pre-transfer mine liabilities exist, the government collects and applies the money through the accounting cutoff, after which the former owner may collect amounts still unrealised.

issues.legal_issue: A former mine owner is not entitled to recover a definite sum directly from the government as mine receipts; the owner’s entitlement is to the residual balance through the statutory payment process after liabilities are dealt with.
material_facts: The former owners claimed specific amounts said to represent outstanding debtor dues, coal despatched during the management period, and a subsidy.
The statutory scheme required accounts to be prepared and audited, creditor claims to be processed, and liabilities to be discharged before any balance was paid to the owner.
The former owners disputed whether the amounts had been properly accounted for.
issues.conclusion: The former owners could not recover a definite or ascertained sum directly. They were entitled to the relevant statements of account and audit, and to payment by the Commissioner of Payments of any balance remaining after liabilities had been discharged. The Court directed appointment of a Commissioner to enquire into the disputed accounting items.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18(2), 19(5)–(7), and 20–27 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 establish the accounting, claims, and payment process. In particular, section 26(1) provides for payment to the owner only of any balance remaining after secured and unsecured creditors’ liabilities have been met. The Court held that the net amount due under section 18(2) is determined through this statutory process, rather than by direct recovery of specific receipts.

predicates.former_owner_accounting_claim: A former mine owner seeks an accounting or payment relating to the management period.
predicates.specific_mine_receipts_are_claimed: The former owner claims direct payment of identified mine receipts or amounts said to be due.
predicates.statutory_liabilities_remain_to_be_proce: Creditor claims and mine liabilities remain subject to the statutory payment process.

issues.definition: When a former owner claims specific mine receipts while statutory liabilities remain to be processed, the owner receives only any residual balance through the Commissioner after those liabilities are dealt with.

issues.legal_issue: A subsidy reimbursement due from the former Coal Board is money due to the mine and may be collected and applied within the statutory mine-accounting scheme rather than paid directly to the former owner.
material_facts: The former owners claimed a subsidy reimbursement from the former Coal Board for hard-rock mining and stowing operations, which remained outstanding in relation to a period before the appointed day.
The High Court had directed the government to pay that subsidy amount to the former owners.
The Supreme Court held that the amount was a due of the mine and set aside that direction.
issues.conclusion: The subsidy was money due to the mine within the meaning of the statutory collection scheme, so the direction requiring direct payment to the former owners was incorrect.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 19(3) and 19(4) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 treat money due to a mine as subject to government collection and use for mine liabilities during the specified period. Relying on Industrial Supplies Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, which construed corresponding provisions of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, the Court held that a subsidy payable by way of reimbursement is like any other due and is money due to the mine.

predicates.nationalisation_mine_accounting_proceedi: The dispute concerns accounting for money due to a mine under a nationalisation scheme.
predicates.reimbursement_is_due_to_mine: A reimbursement is payable to the mine for its operations.
predicates.former_owner_seeks_direct_subsidy_paymen: The former owner seeks direct payment of the reimbursement.

issues.definition: In a mine-accounting dispute, when an operational reimbursement is due to the mine and the former owner seeks it directly, the reimbursement is treated as mine money subject to the statutory accounting process.
